claim: About 36 million people are blind worldwide.
source: About 36 million people are blind worldwide (Bourne et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bourne et al., 2017

claim: In industrialized nations, the dominant causes of blindness are age-related diseases of the eye.
source: In industrialized nations, the dominant causes of blindness are age-related diseases of the eye, all of which disrupt the normal flow of visual data from the eye to the brain.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Age-related diseases of the eye disrupt the normal flow of visual data from the eye to the brain.
source: In industrialized nations, the dominant causes of blindness are age-related diseases of the eye, all of which disrupt the normal flow of visual data from the eye to the brain.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about the mechanism of age-related blindness

claim: Various treatments for blindness involving gene therapy, stem cells, or transplantation are being explored.
source: In some of these cases, biological repair is a potential option, and various treatments are being explored involving gene therapy, stem cells, or transplantation (Scholl et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scholl et al., 2016

claim: The dominant strategy for restoring vision has been to bring the image into the brain through alternate means.
source: However, the dominant strategy for restoring vision has been to bring the image into the brain through alternate means.
evidence: Stated as a summary of the field's approach

claim: Electrical stimulation of surviving cells in the retina is a route for restoring vision.
source: The most direct route is electrical stimulation of surviving cells in the retina (Stingl and Zrenner, 2013; Weiland and Humayun, 2014) or of neurons in the visual cortex (Dobelle et al., 1974).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stingl and Zrenner, 2013; Weiland and Humayun, 2014

claim: Electrical stimulation of neurons in the visual cortex is a route for restoring vision.
source: The most direct route is electrical stimulation of surviving cells in the retina (Stingl and Zrenner, 2013; Weiland and Humayun, 2014) or of neurons in the visual cortex (Dobelle et al., 1974).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dobelle et al., 1974

claim: Translating the raw visual image into touch is an option for vision restoration.
source: Another option involves translating the raw visual image into a different sensory modality (Loomis et al., 2012; Maidenbaum et al., 2014; Proulx et al., 2016), such as touch (Stronks et al., 2016) or hearing (Auvray et al., 2007; Capelle et al., 1998; Meijer, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Loomis et al., 2012; Maidenbaum et al., 2014; Proulx et al., 2016; Stronks et al., 2016

claim: Translating the raw visual image into hearing is an option for vision restoration.
source: Another option involves translating the raw visual image into a different sensory modality (Loomis et al., 2012; Maidenbaum et al., 2014; Proulx et al., 2016), such as touch (Stronks et al., 2016) or hearing (Auvray et al., 2007; Capelle et al., 1998; Meijer, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Auvray et al., 2007; Capelle et al., 1998; Meijer, 1992

claim: None of the existing approaches for vision restoration has enabled any practical recovery of the functions formerly supported by vision.
source: So far, none of these approaches has enabled any practical recovery of the functions formerly supported by vision.
evidence: Stated as a summary assessment of the field

claim: All users of existing vision restoration devices remain legally blind.
source: Despite decades of efforts all users of such devices remain legally blind (Luo and da Cruz, 2016; Stingl et al., 2017; Striem-Amit et al., 2012; Stronks et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Luo and da Cruz, 2016; Stingl et al., 2017; Striem-Amit et al., 2012; Stronks et al., 2016

claim: The human eye takes in about 1 gigabit of raw image information every second.
source: The human eye takes in about 1 gigabit of raw image information every second, whereas our visual system extracts from this just tens of bits to guide our thoughts and actions (Pitkow and Meister, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pitkow and Meister, 2014

claim: The human visual system extracts just tens of bits per second from raw image information to guide thoughts and actions.
source: The human eye takes in about 1 gigabit of raw image information every second, whereas our visual system extracts from this just tens of bits to guide our thoughts and actions (Pitkow and Meister, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pitkow and Meister, 2014

claim: Existing vision restoration approaches seek to transmit the raw image into the brain.
source: All the above approaches seek to transmit the raw image into the brain.
evidence: Stated as a characterization of existing approaches

claim: Transmitting raw images into the brain requires inordinately high data rates.
source: This requires inordinately high data rates.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison between the 1 gigabit input and tens of bits output

claim: None of the technologies available today deliver the high data rate required to retain the relevant details of a scene.
source: None of the technologies available today deliver the high data rate required to retain the relevant details of a scene, nor do they produce a neural code for the image that matches the expectations of the human brain, even given the prodigious degree of adaptive plasticity in the nervous system.
evidence: Stated as an assessment of current technological limitations

claim: Current technologies do not produce a neural code for the image that matches the expectations of the human brain.
source: None of the technologies available today deliver the high data rate required to retain the relevant details of a scene, nor do they produce a neural code for the image that matches the expectations of the human brain, even given the prodigious degree of adaptive plasticity in the nervous system.
evidence: Stated as an assessment of current technological limitations

claim: CARA uses a wearable augmented reality device to give voices to all the relevant objects in the environment.
source: CARA uses a wearable augmented reality device to give voices to all the relevant objects in the environment (Figure 1A).
evidence: Described as the design of the system and shown in Figure 1A

claim: CARA communicates through natural language.
source: Unlike most efforts at scene sonification (Bujacz and Strumiłło, 2016; Csapó and Wersényi, 2013), our system communicates through natural language.
evidence: Stated as a distinguishing feature of CARA compared to other systems

claim: In CARA, each object in the scene can talk to the user with a voice that comes from the object's location.
source: Each object in the scene can talk to the user with a voice that comes from the object's location.
evidence: Described as a feature of the system design

claim: In CARA, the voice's pitch increases as the object gets closer.
source: The voice's pitch increases as the object gets closer.
evidence: Described as a feature of the system design

claim: CARA has a Scan mode where objects call out their names in sequence from left to right.
source: In Scan mode, the objects call out their names in sequence from left to right, offering a quick overview of the scene.
evidence: Described as a feature of the system design

claim: CARA has a Spotlight mode where the object directly in front speaks.
source: In Spotlight mode, the object directly in front speaks, and the user can explore the scene by moving the head.
evidence: Described as a feature of the system design

claim: CARA has a Target mode where the user selects one object that calls repeatedly at the press of a clicker.
source: In Target mode, the user selects one object that calls repeatedly at the press of a clicker.
evidence: Described as a feature of the system design

claim: In CARA, any surface in the space emits a hissing sound as a collision warning when the user gets too close.
source: In addition, any surface in the space emits a hissing sound as a collision warning when the user gets too close (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Described as a feature of the system design and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: CARA is implemented on the Microsoft HoloLens.
source: The system is implemented on the Microsoft HoloLens (Figure 1A), a powerful head-mounted computer designed for augmented reality (Hoffman, 2016).
evidence: Stated as the hardware platform and shown in Figure 1A

claim: The HoloLens scans all surfaces in the environment using video and infrared sensors.
source: The HoloLens scans all surfaces in the environment using video and infrared sensors, creates a 3D map of the surrounding space, and localizes itself within that volume to a precision of a few centimeters (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Described as a capability of the HoloLens hardware

claim: The HoloLens creates a 3D map of the surrounding space.
source: The HoloLens scans all surfaces in the environment using video and infrared sensors, creates a 3D map of the surrounding space, and localizes itself within that volume to a precision of a few centimeters (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Described as a capability of the HoloLens hardware

claim: The HoloLens localizes itself within the scanned volume to a precision of a few centimeters.
source: The HoloLens scans all surfaces in the environment using video and infrared sensors, creates a 3D map of the surrounding space, and localizes itself within that volume to a precision of a few centimeters (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Described as a capability of the HoloLens hardware

claim: Seven blind subjects were recruited for the study.
source: After a preliminary exploration of these methods, we settled on a fixed experimental protocol and recruited seven blind subjects (Figure 1D).
evidence: Stated as the study design and shown in Figure 1D

claim: Subjects heard a short explanation of what to expect before using CARA.
source: Subjects heard a short explanation of what to expect, then donned the HoloLens and launched into a series of four fully automated tasks without experimenter involvement.
evidence: Described as part of the experimental protocol

claim: No training sessions were provided to subjects before using CARA.
source: No training sessions were provided, and all the data were gathered within a 2 hr visit.
evidence: Stated as part of the experimental protocol

claim: All data were gathered within a 2 hr visit.
source: No training sessions were provided, and all the data were gathered within a 2 hr visit.
evidence: Stated as part of the experimental protocol

claim: All subjects found localizing virtual sound sources a reasonable request.
source: All subjects found this a reasonable request and oriented surprisingly well, with an accuracy of 3–12 degrees (standard deviation across trials, Figure 1C).
evidence: Reported as an observation from the object localization task

claim: Subjects oriented to virtual sound sources with an accuracy of 3–12 degrees standard deviation.
source: All subjects found this a reasonable request and oriented surprisingly well, with an accuracy of 3–12 degrees (standard deviation across trials, Figure 1C).
evidence: Measured in the object localization task and shown in Figure 1C

claim: Several subjects had a systematic pointing bias to one or the other side of the target ranging from −9 to +13 degrees.
source: Several subjects had a systematic pointing bias to one or the other side of the target (−9 to +13 deg, Figure 1C), but no attempt was made to correct for this bias.
evidence: Measured in the object localization task and shown in Figure 1C

claim: Users can accurately localize the virtual voices generated by HoloLens.
source: These results show that users can accurately localize the virtual voices generated by HoloLens, even though the software used a generic head-related transfer function without customization.
evidence: Concluded from the object localization task results

claim: The HoloLens software used a generic head-related transfer function without customization.
source: These results show that users can accurately localize the virtual voices generated by HoloLens, even though the software used a generic head-related transfer function without customization.
evidence: Stated as a feature of the implementation

claim: All subjects performed remarkably well in recalling the arrangement of all objects in the spatial memory task.
source: All subjects performed remarkably well, correctly recalling the arrangement of all objects (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with just one error (1/28 trials).
evidence: Measured in the spatial memory task and shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Subjects made only one error in 28 trials in the first round of the spatial memory task.
source: All subjects performed remarkably well, correctly recalling the arrangement of all objects (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with just one error (1/28 trials).
evidence: Measured in the spatial memory task

claim: Subjects reproduced the absolute positions of objects from memory to an average accuracy of ~15 deg rms deviation.
source: Even the overall scale of the scene and the absolute positions of the objects were reproduced well from memory, to an average accuracy of ~15 deg (rms deviation from true position, Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Measured in the spatial memory task and shown in Figure 2C-D

claim: In the second round of the spatial memory task, three subjects made a mistake.
source: In a second round, we shuffled the object positions and repeated the task. Here three of the subjects made a mistake, presumably owing to interference with the memory formed on the previous round.
evidence: Measured in the spatial memory task

claim: Mistakes in the second round of the spatial memory task were presumably due to interference with the memory formed on the previous round.
source: In a second round, we shuffled the object positions and repeated the task. Here three of the subjects made a mistake, presumably owing to interference with the memory formed on the previous round.
evidence: Speculated as an explanation for the observed errors

claim: Sighted subjects who inspected the scene visually performed similarly to blind subjects on the recall task.
source: Sighted subjects who inspected the scene visually performed similarly on the recall task (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Measured as a comparison and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Active exploration of object voices builds an effective mental representation of the scene that supports subsequent recall and orientation.
source: These experiments suggest that active exploration of object voices builds an effective mental representation of the scene that supports subsequent recall and orientation in the environment.
evidence: Concluded from the spatial memory task results

claim: All subjects found the chair in the direct navigation task after walking essentially straight-line trajectories.
source: All subjects found the chair after walking essentially straight-line trajectories (Figure 3B–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Measured in the direct navigation task and shown in Figure 3B-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Most users followed a two-phase strategy in direct navigation: first localize the voice by turning in place, then walk swiftly toward it.
source: Most users followed a two-phase strategy: first localize the voice by turning in place, then walk swiftly toward it (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Observed in the direct navigation task and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-E

claim: On rare occasions (~5 of 139 trials), a subject started walking in the opposite direction, then reversed course.
source: On rare occasions (~5 of 139 trials), a subject started walking in the opposite direction, then reversed course (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), presumably owing to ambiguities in azimuthal sound cues (McAnally and Martin, 2014).
evidence: Measured in the direct navigation task and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: Occasional wrong-direction starts were presumably owing to ambiguities in azimuthal sound cues.
source: On rare occasions (~5 of 139 trials), a subject started walking in the opposite direction, then reversed course (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), presumably owing to ambiguities in azimuthal sound cues (McAnally and Martin, 2014).
evidence: Speculated as an explanation with citation to McAnally and Martin, 2014

claim: For all subjects, the average trajectory in direct navigation was only 11–25% longer than the straight-line distance.
source: Regardless, for all subjects the average trajectory was only 11–25% longer than the straight-line distance (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Measured in the direct navigation task and shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Searches without CARA using only a cane took on average eight times longer than with CARA.
source: For comparison, we asked subjects to find a real chair in the same space using only their usual walking aid (Figure 3D). These searches took on average eight times longer and covered 13 times the distance needed with CARA.
evidence: Measured as a comparison in the direct navigation task and shown in Figure 3D

claim: Searches without CARA using only a cane covered 13 times the distance needed with CARA.
source: For comparison, we asked subjects to find a real chair in the same space using only their usual walking aid (Figure 3D). These searches took on average eight times longer and covered 13 times the distance needed with CARA.
evidence: Measured as a comparison in the direct navigation task and shown in Figure 3D

claim: Subjects weaved through virtual obstacles without collision using the alarm sounds.
source: In a related series of experiments we encumbered the path to the target with several virtual obstacles. Using the alarm sounds, our subjects weaved through the obstacles without collision (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Measured in obstacle avoidance experiments and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D

claim: Subjects reported that steering towards a voice is a natural function that can be performed automatically.
source: Informal reports from the subjects confirmed that steering towards a voice is a natural function that can be performed automatically, leaving attentional bandwidth for other activities.
evidence: Reported by subjects during experiments

claim: Some subjects carried on a conversation while following CARA.
source: For example, some subjects carried on a conversation while following CARA.
evidence: Observed during experiments

claim: All seven subjects completed the long-range navigation trajectory on the first attempt.
source: All seven subjects completed the trajectory on the first attempt (Figure 4B–C, Video 1).
evidence: Measured in the long-range guided navigation task and shown in Figure 4B-C and Video 1

claim: The long-range navigation task required on average 119 s (range 73–159 s).
source: On average, this task required 119 s (range 73–159 s), a tolerable investment for finding an office in an unfamiliar building (Figure 4E).
evidence: Measured in the long-range guided navigation task and shown in Figure 4E

claim: The median distance walked by subjects in long-range navigation was 36 m.
source: The median distance walked by the subjects was 36 m (Figure 4D), slightly shorter (~1%) than the path programmed for the virtual guide, because the subjects can cut corners (Figure 4C).
evidence: Measured in the long-range guided navigation task and shown in Figure 4D

claim: The median distance walked by subjects was slightly shorter (~1%) than the path programmed for the virtual guide because subjects can cut corners.
source: The median distance walked by the subjects was 36 m (Figure 4D), slightly shorter (~1%) than the path programmed for the virtual guide, because the subjects can cut corners (Figure 4C).
evidence: Measured in the long-range guided navigation task and explained by observation shown in Figure 4C

claim: On the stairs, subjects proceeded at ~60% of their free-walking speed.
source: The subjects' speed varied with difficulty along the route, but even on the stairs they proceeded at ~60% of their free-walking speed (Figure 4F).
evidence: Measured in the long-range guided navigation task and shown in Figure 4F

claim: On arriving at the office, one subject remarked 'That was fun! When can I get one?'
source: On arriving at the office, one subject remarked "That was fun! When can I get one?".
evidence: Reported as a direct quote from a subject

claim: YOLO will readily identify objects in a real time video feed that match one of 9000 categories.
source: For example, YOLO (Redmon and Farhadi, 2018) will readily identify objects in a real time video feed that match one of 9000 categories.
evidence: Stated as a capability of YOLO with citation to Redmon and Farhadi, 2018

claim: YOLO already runs on the HoloLens.
source: The algorithm already runs on the HoloLens and we are adopting it for use within CARA (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Stated as a technical implementation and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F

claim: Using CARA, subjects mostly used the Target mode to efficiently find the desired object in the virtual living room.
source: On the first task, the subject stood in the middle of the virtual living room and was asked to locate one of the objects and point at it with the head. With CARA, subjects mostly used the Target mode to efficiently find the desired object, and located it based on the 3D sound cues, with a typical aiming error of 10 degrees (Figure 5B, bias of −0.2–13 deg, accuracy 4.5–27 deg).
evidence: Measured in the benchmarking task and shown in Figure 5B

claim: With CARA, subjects located objects with a typical aiming error of 10 degrees (bias of −0.2–13 deg, accuracy 4.5–27 deg) in the virtual living room.
source: With CARA, subjects mostly used the Target mode to efficiently find the desired object, and located it based on the 3D sound cues, with a typical aiming error of 10 degrees (Figure 5B, bias of −0.2–13 deg, accuracy 4.5–27 deg).
evidence: Measured in the benchmarking task and shown in Figure 5B

claim: With vOICe, subjects reported great difficulty at identifying objects in the virtual living room.
source: With vOICe, subjects reported great difficulty at identifying objects, despite the earlier opportunity to practice with visual feedback.
evidence: Reported by subjects in the benchmarking task

claim: With vOICe, subjects' aiming choices were statistically consistent with a uniform random distribution in the virtual living room.
source: Their aiming choices were statistically consistent with a uniform random distribution (Figure 5B).
evidence: Measured in the benchmarking task and shown in Figure 5B

claim: Using CARA, subjects found the chair efficiently in the virtual living room, requiring only 10 s on average.
source: Using CARA, subjects found the chair efficiently, requiring only 10 s on average (Figure 5C).
evidence: Measured in the benchmarking task and shown in Figure 5C

claim: Using vOICe, most subjects meandered through the arena in the chair-finding task.
source: Using vOICe, most subjects meandered through the arena, on occasion encountering the chair by accident.
evidence: Observed in the benchmarking task

claim: Only one subject was able to steer toward the chair using vOICe.
source: Only one subject was able to steer toward the chair (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed in the benchmarking task and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: None of the subjects were able to complete 20 trials within the 60 s time limit using vOICe for the chair-finding task.
source: None of the subjects were able to complete 20 trials within the 60 s time limit.
evidence: Measured in the benchmarking task

claim: Using CARA, subjects found the key efficiently in the virtual living room.
source: Using CARA, subjects found the key efficiently (Figure 5D).
evidence: Measured in the benchmarking task and shown in Figure 5D

claim: Using vOICe, none of the subjects were able to locate the key in the virtual living room.
source: Using vOICe none of the subjects were able to locate the key (Figure 5D), although two of them encountered it once by accident (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Measured in the benchmarking task and shown in Figure 5D

claim: Two subjects encountered the key once by accident using vOICe.
source: Using vOICe none of the subjects were able to locate the key (Figure 5D), although two of them encountered it once by accident (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Measured in the benchmarking task and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Naive subjects performed well on real-world tasks using CARA, but not using vOICe.
source: Naive subjects performed well on these real-world tasks using CARA, but not using vOICe.
evidence: Concluded from the benchmarking task results

claim: Interpreting the vOICe sounds is very non-intuitive.
source: It should be said that interpreting the vOICe sounds is very non-intuitive.
evidence: Stated as an observation about vOICe

claim: Extensive training with vOICe confers blind subjects with some ability to distinguish high contrast shapes on a clean background.
source: Extensive training with vOICe confers blind subjects with some ability to distinguish high contrast shapes on a clean background (Auvray et al., 2007; Striem-Amit et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Auvray et al., 2007; Striem-Amit et al., 2012

claim: The principal reason sighted people rely on vision much more than audition is that almost all objects in the world emit useful light signals almost all the time, whereas useful sound signals from our surroundings are few and sporadic.
source: The principal reason sighted people rely on vision much more than audition is that almost all objects in the world emit useful light signals almost all the time, whereas useful sound signals from our surroundings are few and sporadic.
evidence: Stated as an explanation based on general knowledge

claim: CARA can change the calculus such that all the relevant objects emit easily interpretable sounds.
source: CARA can change this calculus fundamentally, such that all the relevant objects emit easily interpretable sounds.
evidence: Stated as a capability of CARA

claim: Extended use of CARA may eventually produce subjective qualia that resemble the feeling of seeing.
source: It is conceivable that the extended use of such an intuitive modality eventually produces subjective qualia that resemble the feeling of seeing.
evidence: Stated as a speculative possibility

claim: Blind people report that outdoor navigation is supported by many services but these all fall away when one enters a building.
source: Blind people report that outdoor navigation is supported by many services (access vans, GPS, mobile phones with navigation apps) but these all fall away when one enters a building (Karimi, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Karimi, 2015

claim: In its present form CARA can already function as a guide in a large public building, hotel, or mall.
source: In its present form CARA can already function in this underserved domain, for example as a guide in a large public building, hotel, or mall.
evidence: Stated as a current capability of CARA

claim: No physical modifications of the space are required for CARA to function.
source: No physical modifications of the space are required.
evidence: Stated as a feature of CARA

claim: Naive visitors could pick up a CARA device at a building entrance and begin using it in minutes.
source: Thanks to the intuitive interface, naive visitors could pick up a device at the building entrance and begin using it in minutes.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing minimal training requirements

claim: The subjects represent a small but realistic sample of the expected blind user population.
source: In this context, recall that our subjects were chosen without prescreening, including cases of early and late blindness and various hearing deficits (Figure 1D): They represent a small but realistic sample of the expected blind user population.
evidence: Stated as a characterization of the subject sample with reference to Figure 1D

claim: Localization errors of the HoloLens amount to <4 cm.
source: Localization errors of the HoloLens amount to <4 cm (Liu et al., 2018), which is insignificant compared to the distance measures reported in our study, and smaller than the line width in the graphs of trajectories in Figures 3 and 4.
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2018

claim: The Microsoft HoloLens Development Edition currently costs $3000.
source: The hardware platform used in the research – Microsoft HoloLens Development Edition – currently costs $3000.
evidence: Stated as factual information about the hardware cost

claim: The current HoloLens weighs 579 g.
source: The current HoloLens weighs 579 g.
evidence: Stated as factual information about the hardware

claim: The current HoloLens battery supports the system functions for 2–5 hr.
source: The current battery supports our system functions for 2–5 hr, sufficient for the indoor excursions we envision in public buildings, led by the 'virtual guide'.
evidence: Stated as factual information about the hardware

claim: Occasional loss of tracking or localization errors occur particularly when the environment lacks visual features such as a narrow space with white walls.
source: While in most indoor scenarios that we have tested the tracking of HoloLens was reliable and precise, we have encountered occasional loss of tracking or localization errors. This occurs particularly when the environment lacks visual features such as a narrow space with white walls.
evidence: Observed during testing of the system
